newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Yilmaz is unlikely hero of secularists.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Yilmaz is unlikely hero of secularists.

text.p: Turkish conservative leader Mesut Yilmaz, appointed prime minister by President Suleyman Demirel on Monday, is a political tortoise among hares.
Islamist ex-prime minister Necmettin Erbakan enthuses in flowing phrases about a "Just Order". Yilmaz's bitter rival conservative Tansu Ciller exhorts her country "forward into Europe".
But Yilmaz, slow-spoken and earnest, never seems to stir the blood despite his new-found role as hero of the country's secularists.
He has, however, kept his conservative free-market Motherland Party on an even keel in the turmoil of Turkish politics, although analysts say his years in opposition have been lack-lustre.
Motherland is the second-biggest party in parliament.
Crucially, he has also managed to earn himself a reputation for being more committed to Turkey's secular tradition than his two main rivals.
The U.S.-educated Ciller last year allied herself with Erbakan's Islam-based Welfare Party to create a government that deeply disturbed Turkey's powerful military.
Yilmaz turned down an alliance with the Islamists after lengthy negotiations last year.
The soldiers believe that Erbakan's tolerance for rising religious activism is a serious threat to the country.
Erbakan bowed to armed forces pressure on June 18 and resigned. Two days later Demirel charged Yilmaz with forming a government that would keep the Islamists out of power.
Now, at 50, still young for a Turkish leader, Yilmaz is poised to ask for a parliamentary vote of confidence in his new government.
He says his latest coalition has been formed "with the aim of strengthening secularism and democracy." It will be his third shot at building a lasting government.

He led the country for three months in 1991 until a general election defeat by the True Path Party, then led by Demirel who became president in May 1993 and left his post to Ciller, a U.S.-educated economist.
It was the fierce animosity between Yilmaz and Ciller that brought about the downfall of a 1996 coalition between the pair after another three months.
That coalition's collapse helped Islamists take a lion's share in government for the first time in Turkey's modern history.
The two conservative parties are close on policy but the leaders are poles apart. Ciller is a dramatic, instinctive political survivor, and Yilmaz measured, thoughtful and, some say, a tad boring.
Their rivalry has defined Yilmaz's recent career. He has spent many years -- largely unsuccessfully -- attempting to frustrate Ciller and pin corruption charges on her.
But he has had success in poaching deputies away from Ciller's party. The defections have made his government's prospects in the vote of confidence look much healthier.
Yilmaz took control of Motherland in April 1993, after the sudden death of its founder and later Turkish president Turgut Ozal. He has since distanced the party from Ozal and his powerful family.
Born into a wealthy family in the Black Sea town of Rize, Yilmaz entered parliament in 1983 after three years of army rule that cracked down on extremist political violence.
Previously he had held managerial positions in various private enterprises in chemicals, textiles and transport.
Yilmaz, who helped found Motherland, was state minister and then tourism and culture minister in the 1983 civilian government founded by then prime minister Ozal.
He later served as foreign minister for three years until he resigned in a policy dispute with then premier Yildirim Akbulut, widely seen as a tool for Ozal's continuing influence.
Yilmaz is a political science graduate from Ankara University. He is married, has two children and speaks English and German.
